title: Trending Kids' Toys UK
short: The toys and franchises UK kids are asking for this year, from Lego and Pokemon to plush and STEM building sets.
intro: Every year a handful of toys and franchises dominate kids' wish lists, and this year is no exception. This guide rounds up what Which? and John Lewis identify as the trending toys for 2026, spanning ages, budgets and interests, along with the safety marks worth checking before you buy.

guide.q: What safety marks should I check before buying a toy?
guide.a: Look for a UKCA or CE mark, both of which indicate the toy meets UK or EU safety standards, plus a UK contact address on the packaging. The voluntary Lion Mark from the British Toy & Hobby Association shows the maker follows safety and ethical practice standards beyond the legal minimum.

guide.q: What does the '0-3' warning symbol mean?
guide.a: This symbol warns that a toy contains small parts or other features that pose a choking or safety hazard for children under 3, and toys unsuitable for under-3s are legally required to carry this warning. It's a safety warning rather than a general recommendation, so check it even if a child seems capable of playing with the toy.

guide.q: Are toys from online marketplaces as safe as those from shops?
guide.a: Not necessarily. The British Toy & Hobby Association has reported serious safety issues with a high proportion of toys bought through some online marketplaces, often from third-party sellers rather than the platform itself. Buying from an established retailer or brand's own listing reduces this risk.

guide.q: Are trending or licensed toys worth the extra cost over generic alternatives?
guide.a: Licensed and trending toys often cost more for the branding, but many also include genuine functional extras, like Lego's Smart Play interactive bricks here. If budget matters more than the specific character or brand, a generic or own-brand equivalent with similar play features can be better value.
